argument: Under stable conditions, species that depend on exactly the same limiting resource and interact identically cannot coexist indefinitely; one excludes the other. Coexistence requires differentiation, temporal or spatial variability, predation, trade-offs, immigration, or other stabilizing/equalizing mechanisms.
boundary: Natural communities rarely satisfy identical-niche, equilibrium, and closed-system assumptions.
Neutral dynamics and slow exclusion can mimic coexistence.
Multiple resources and nonlinear interactions change outcomes.
claim: Under stable conditions, species that depend on exactly the same limiting resource and interact identically cannot coexist indefinitely; one excludes the other. Coexistence requires differentiation, temporal or spatial variability, predation, trade-offs, immigration, or other stabilizing/equalizing mechanisms.
interpretation: Use as a boundary condition, not a universal claim that similar species cannot coexist. Principia should identify the limiting resource and stabilizing mechanism.

argument: When a system is represented by a functional $J[u]$, stationary points satisfying $\delta J=0$ yield Euler–Lagrange equations and boundary conditions. Variational formulations unify differential equations, optimization, mechanics, geometry, and approximation.
boundary: A stationary point need not be a minimum or stable.
Not every governing equation has a useful scalar variational formulation.
Boundary regularity, admissible function spaces, and differentiability assumptions matter.
